lessons.title: Heat Stroke: Cool First, Fast
lessons.summary: hyperthermia + CNS dysfunction after heat exposure is a cooling emergency.

sections.title: 1) Definition concept
paragraphs: Heat stroke is severe heat illness with marked hyperthermia and central neurologic dysfunction; exertional and classic forms have different populations but both require rapid cooling.

sections.title: 2) Organ injury
paragraphs: Coagulopathy, rhabdomyolysis, hepatic/renal injury, shock and electrolyte disturbances can develop.

sections.title: 3) Cooling
paragraphs: Immediate active cooling is the priority; cold-water immersion is highly effective for exertional heat stroke when feasible, with alternative evaporative/conductive methods as context dictates.

sections.title: 4) Avoid delay
paragraphs: Do not postpone cooling for transport or diagnostic certainty when heat stroke is clear and safe cooling can begin.

lessons.title: Accidental Hypothermia: Gentle Handling, Rewarming & Arrest
lessons.summary: cold patients can have profound bradycardia and altered consciousness; physiology and resuscitation differ.

sections.title: 1) Staging by physiology
paragraphs: Mild: shivering/alert. Moderate/severe: declining consciousness, shivering may stop, bradycardia/hypoventilation and arrhythmia risk increase.

sections.title: 2) Handling
paragraphs: Move gently, prevent further heat loss, remove wet clothing when safe, insulate and use appropriate active/passive rewarming.

sections.title: 3) Cardiac arrest
paragraphs: Pulse may be very slow and hard to detect; follow hypothermia-specific resuscitation guidance for defibrillation/medications and transport to extracorporeal-capable center when indicated.

sections.title: 4) Rewarming choices
paragraphs: External vs internal rewarming depends on severity/circulation. Avoid rough handling and unnecessary extremity warming in severe hypothermia.

lessons.title: Drowning: Hypoxia First
lessons.summary: drowning arrest is primarily hypoxic; ventilation is unusually important compared with primary cardiac arrest.

sections.title: 1) Pathophysiology
paragraphs: Submersion/immersion causes airway impairment, hypoxemia and potentially cardiac arrest. Aspiration and lung injury may persist after rescue.

sections.title: 2) Rescue priorities
paragraphs: Scene/water safety first. Begin ventilation/CPR promptly once safe and indicated; AED/defibrillation follows standard principles.

sections.title: 3) Do not “drain water”
paragraphs: Routine abdominal thrusts/Heimlich to remove water are not recommended and delay ventilation; use suction if material obstructs the airway.

sections.title: 4) Post-rescue
paragraphs: Persistent cough, hypoxemia, dyspnea or altered mental state requires medical evaluation; hypothermia can coexist.

lessons.title: Snakebite: Envenomation Recognition & Safe First Aid
lessons.summary: avoid harmful traditional first aid; immobilize, monitor and identify syndrome/antivenom need.

sections.title: 1) Local vs systemic effects
paragraphs: Pain/swelling, coagulopathy/bleeding, neuroparalysis, rhabdomyolysis, shock and renal injury vary by species.

sections.title: 2) First aid
paragraphs: Keep patient calm, minimize exertion, immobilize affected limb in a functional position and transport. Remove rings/tight items as swelling evolves.

sections.title: 3) Avoid
paragraphs: No cutting/sucking, ice, electric shock or tight arterial tourniquet. Pressure immobilization is species/region dependent and should follow local guidance.

sections.title: 4) Antivenom
paragraphs: Antivenom is for clinically significant envenomation and requires trained monitoring for reactions; species-appropriate Thai protocols are essential.

lessons.title: Electrical Injury & Lightning
lessons.summary: skin burns can underestimate internal injury; scene electricity is the first hazard.

sections.title: 1) Scene safety
paragraphs: Do not touch patient until electrical source is isolated. High-voltage scenes may have step potential and require utility/fire rescue.

sections.title: 2) Injury mechanisms
paragraphs: Arrhythmia, respiratory arrest, deep muscle injury, fractures/falls, burns and rhabdomyolysis. Lightning can cause simultaneous cardiac and respiratory arrest.

sections.title: 3) Monitoring
paragraphs: ECG and evaluation are important after significant current exposure, syncope, chest symptoms, abnormal ECG or high-voltage injury.

sections.title: 4) Lightning triage
paragraphs: In mass lightning casualty situations, patients in arrest may deserve early resuscitation because respiratory arrest can precede potentially reversible cardiac arrest.
